author: Gustave Flaubert
introFa: کتاب «Sentimental Education» نوشته Gustave Flaubert یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح C1 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «Sentimental Education»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

content: Book Review BILINGUAL AESTHETICS: A NEW SENTIMENTAL EDUCATION, by Doris Sommer. Durham and London: Duke University Press, 2004, 254 pp. Doris Sommer’s new work Bilingual Aesthetics is the sort of book that takes one by surprise—and for good reason. Filled with punning twists, and itself a valorizer of word games and magic, this work has not a lot to do with bilin- gualism (in the standard sense), not a lot to do with aesthetics (again, in the standard academic sense), but a great deal to do with both. Whether the title is read (and Sommer’s point is to for- ward the notion of alternate readings) as the aesthetics of bilingualism or as an account of what a bilingual might make of aesthetics, there is a startling amount of content in the work. Briefly, Sommer essays to make the case that our multicultural society is distinctly better off for being multi- cultural and multilingual (or at least, in some threatening sense, emergently bi- lingual) because the literal bilingual has a distinct advantage over her or his monolingual counterpart. The bi- lingual can play language games, and those games shock, amuse, or jolt— whatever it is that they do, they rouse us out of any state of intellectual torpor into which we might have fallen and they serve to make us all individuals who, in Du Bois’ memorable phrase, have “double consciousness.” Thus Sommer does in fact mean for her title to be read in at least two ways: Her work attempts to valorize and vin- dicate a sort of unofficial bilingualism (one of the blurbs on the back of the paperback edition begins by saying “Knowing a second language entails some unease . . . ”), while she also at- tempts to let us in on the notion that there is an aesthetic that develops from the use of more than one code. Sommer plays remarkably on all these concepts: She is familiar with the standard, overt scholarship on bilingualism—she can cite work by sociolinguists and others. At the same time, as an author known for previous work on literature, espe- cially with regard to Latin America, she is also familiar with much of the stan- dard historical work in aesthetics, in- cluding Kant. Citing thinkers such as Kenji Hakuta, William J. Bennett, Wittgenstein, and Elena Poniatowska, Sommer leaves the reader somewhat bedazzled and breathless but better off for having read her work. Her overall thesis, if one may at- tempt to employ such a phrase, is that bilingualism and code-switching create for us the same sort of uneasiness and inevitable access to the unconscious that works of art and literature pro- duce—and that the edginess that is a concomitant of code-switching is ben- eficial. Her first chapter “Choose and Lose” reminds Americans that the United States has always been a multi- lingual place and focuses on how much can be gained from attempting to for- ward the notion. If there is any diffi- culty to Sommer’s work, it is that she practices what she preaches. Every page demands much of the reader, since every page itself engages in the

122 Book Review sort of rapid-fire twisting and switch- ing that Sommer is trying to support as the ground for a new aesthetic consciousness. Early on, Sommer gives us the following: Complaints about the danger to national coherence [of multi- or bilingualism] can be downright funny . . . . [One irate journalist wrote:] “How can immigrants identify with America if they can’t read Lincoln’s words in the language in which they were spoken? Will we devolve from E pluribus unum (out of many, one) to a multicultural boarding house, . . . ?” No need to be upset at this harangue. It’s obviously a joke, even if the author missed it (a common asymmetry in bilingual humor). Notice that the translation from Latin as- sumes that English-only citi- zens don’t understand the very slogan they hold dear. (p. 26) But of course the joke is to some ex- tent on Sommer and on all of us, as she no doubt intends. It is highly unlikely that the journalist did get the humor, and the only funny part of the entire tirade is that we—assuming we have enough formal education—may be able to make something out of it, al- though (to top it all off) Latin is not currently a spoken language. Sommer’s work proceeds in this di- rection, using doses of postmodern irony and detachment to address the serious issues posed by the onslaught of “English-only” educators and poli- ticians. There is no question that Sommer is on the right track about the Freudian delights of knowing more than one language, of being able to code-switch, of being one up on one’s audience, and so forth. (Her third chapter is titled “Irritate the State.”) But there is a downside to the entire controversy and the quagmire it has left, despite the joy that Sommer es- pouses. Many immigrants and children born in the United States will learn to code-switch, and they will be able to enjoy the “games” that Sommer ad- mires and recommends. But in general these will not be immigrants who are at the socioeconomic bottom—for them, there will be little joy in learning a smattering of English by working at McDonald’s or cutting meat at the local packing house. By the same token, many middle-class native-born Ameri- cans who come from monolingual backgrounds will eventually become bilingual—and more power to them, particularly if the second language is Spanish, which might in the future (a future acknowledged by Sommer, al- though she seems to find it somewhat unlikely) become the second official language, as French and English have achieved co-language status in Canada. But again this will no doubt be a privi- lege largely restricted to the middle- class. English-only monolinguals in Appalachia will have a remarkably dif- ficult time navigating the school sys- tem with the language they already have, given that they will be told many times that their code has little or no value and that they should learn “standard English.” At the beginning of her work, Sommer shows sensitivity to these is- sues and remarks upon the degree to which “bilingualism” is itself a phe- nomenon of social class and hence not something easily defined or codifi- able. Nevertheless the work proceeds on the assumption that the desired bi- lingualism is that achievable by the formally educated individual who can enjoy the variety of language games with which Wittgenstein, among others, familiarized us. Despite these shortcomings—bilin- gualism not readily being an enjoyable topic for many of America’s paid

Book Review 123 educators, particularly in the pri- mary grades—Sommer’s work brings enough freshness to this somewhat tired concept that it is more than worth reading. Her insight that the discom- fort that we feel as we plod along with our second or third language (either verbally or in written format) will readily give way to merriment on those occasions when we find ourselves navi- gating the twists and turns is valuable, and there is no question that her con- tention—taken directly from Freud— that language use, joking, and the dis- play of wit are all related is a valuable one. Indeed some of the most remark- able material in the work is constituted by Sommer’s own bilingual range and by her repertoire of jokes that rely on the crucial concepts of misunderstand- ing, failure to attend to code-switching, and the like. (Particularly valuable are the two elaborate switching routines taken from the frontispiece to Chapter 1—the reader will no doubt wonder why he or she has not heard these hilarious tales before.) It would be easy to say that Sommer’s work is suited to the class- room, particularly given the timeliness of this topic in educational circles. The truth is that very few graduate schools of education, for example, will be able to use this work—unless the school in question already has a core philosophy-of-education component, this work is likely to seem entirely too recondite. But her work can be used in the sort of class for which she probably intended it—a literature or philosophy seminar where aesthetics itself is a standard topic and where something above and beyond the routine might prove enlivening and useful. For Sommer’s point ultimately is that the double take is at the heart of much aes- thetic enjoyment (and this does not ex- clude of course the visual arts). Some literary traditions will be more affected than others, but there is no question that the traditions of Latin America (and especially of Mexico, of which Sommer shows heightened awareness) themselves, without advertence to English, frequently rely on bilingual codes. (Mexico has an entire philoso- phy of the mestizaje that involves all sorts of material, including linguistic material, taken from the indigenous.) Any course dealing with this mate- rial would find Sommer’s new work extremely helpful. Sommer has constructed for us an elaborate sort of joke. In working through what initially appears to be a standard academic text, our senses are awakened and our taste for other lan- guages renewed. Perhaps inevitably the joke is on us, and there is absolutely no doubt that we deserved it. Jane Duran Department of Philosophy University of California, Santa Barbara
